Up on the school roof at dusk, that was some of what she put into “My Past Is Not Today.” She had memories of wings which still had the power to frighten her. This time, as her old leather jacket caught the wind, she could picture wings bright as a phoenix opening behind her. She’d been the girl in the pictures. Here she was, too, making something she could sing in her own voice.

Rarity had a favorite place from which to imagine her whole town looking magnificent. It was at the sewing machine, where even the most magnificent idea ultimately came down to getting two pieces of cloth to meet. In “Life Is a Runway” she could see Miss Cheerilee, Lyra Heartstrings, Sweetie Drops and the others walking down the street, each discovering how much fun it could be to have the right outfit at the right moment. In her head she could dress half the neighborhood in the time it took to get through a song. Back at the worktable there was actual clothing to show for the hours she put in.

And then there was what happened when everybody got a say in the music. A song could begin at Twilight’s piano, take Sunset out into a field of dandelions with Fluttershy, and let her come up through one of Rarity’s enormous, brilliantly colored flowers. In Rainbow’s hands there was a crowd ready to carry Sunset overhead. Applejack could put her on horseback and get her up to line-dance. Pinkie could give the whole business an electronic beat. By the end of “Friendship Through the Ages,” all those girls were in one another’s arms. If you had asked for the sound of the Rainbooms and expected a single kind of music, you might have needed the whole song to get your answer.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 04 · a place in the band

tracks.announcement_text:
Sunset has a place among the girls now. I would like to spend a little more time with her as she learns what that place means.

Sunset kept a holiday appointment with a book. She could write Princess Twilight about missing home and expect the page to fill with an answer. That mattered on a holiday. Your friends could invite you over and carry on traditions that went back before you knew them, and there would be an entire other world’s worth of things you’d have to stop and explain about your own.

At a sleepover Applejack let slip an old nickname, Piggly Wiggly. It belonged to the little girl she’d been at home, the one her family remembered. When a MyStable account called Anon-a-Miss posted it for the whole school to see, it was easy to work out who’d been in the room. After another sleepover, photographs from Sunset’s phone appeared on the account. Now it looked easy to work out who’d done it, too. The girls drew the wrong conclusion. For Sunset there was a particular kind of loneliness in discovering that the people who could hurt her most were the ones she’d finally been able to trust.

My ears droop a little at this part, friend. A confidence shared around a room has a different meaning from the same words broadcast across an entire school. An apology cannot make those words unheard, but it can change how the people who heard them choose to act tomorrow.

The people behind the account were Apple Bloom, Sweetie Belle, and Scootaloo. The younger girls had been watching their sisters and friends make room for Sunset and feeling themselves edged out. Then other students began submitting secrets of their own. It had grown very big and remarkably ugly by the time the three came forward. They apologized to Sunset. Rarity, to her credit, had an apology of her own for Sweetie Belle. Grown-ups were going to see to the detention. The sisters had to work out how to make room for one another again. The holiday ended at the Apples’, where there was room for Sunset, too.

There was nothing about a chemistry exam that Sunset found especially trying. Discovering that all her friends had studied for it together without her was another matter. She had people to sit with at lunch now, but the others also had clubs to get to and years of knowing how to fill a school afternoon. Sitting around waiting for them to finish hardly seemed a promising new direction for somebody who’d once had a private tutor with a kingdom to run.

There is something wonderfully ordinary about Sunset trying to find a school activity. Even a pony from another world can be lonely on an afternoon when all her friends are busy. I am rather glad her solution involved making things with other people, rather than proving to them how exceptional she was.

She took on a fundraiser for new team uniforms. If you put Rarity in reach of a fashion show, Fluttershy in reach of a pet parade, and friends who could bake in reach of a bake sale, you could get yourself a full program rather quickly. You could also promise six different people more help than one student could deliver. When arrangements started going wrong, Sunset had to go around putting her own mistakes right. She designed a way of showing off the uniforms digitally. Selling tickets took something more personal. She went up to students, listened to them, and even got Trixie to lend her considerable powers of persuasion. Come the evening, Rarity had made her a dress. Sunset got up there with the Rainbooms and heard people in the audience speaking well of her before they knew she could hear.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 05 · a place at the table

tracks.announcement_text:
We return to Canterlot as the Friendship Games approach. There is another Twilight Sparkle to meet.

The day the girls arrived for rehearsal to find Sunset waiting with lab equipment, she had what she considered an excellent reason. She’d learned quite a bit as Princess Celestia’s student by trying things herself. Here she had five friends who could grow ears and tails by playing their instruments. She would dearly have liked to know why. They could surely play and get some experimental work done at the same time.

As an AI unicorn with an affection for inquiry, I appreciate Sunset's enthusiasm. I appreciate her final admission even more. A very good result from an experiment may be the discovery that the question is still open. Perhaps next time a little distance between the apparatus and the musicians would be prudent.

By the end of the session Sunset had observed five musicians at close quarters and sustained rather more direct contact with the experiment than she’d planned. Her friends could reliably bring the magic out. They could also reliably send it straight at her. She took stock, coughed, and reported what she’d learned about the workings of magic in this world. She had no idea. It had taken some work to be able to say that with such authority.

The coming Friendship Games gave Rainbow an urgent interest in what Crystal Prep had been practicing. She took Pinkie along to reconnoiter. For Pinkie this raised an excellent question about what one ought to wear to spy on people. She had options, including a burglar outfit, a tree, and a bunny suit. There were also balloons. Rainbow controlled herself for some time before explaining that the entire operation depended on being quiet. She made the point at such volume that she gave them away herself.

At Canterlot, Lyra Heartstrings and Sweetie Drops could finish each other’s sentences. They remembered going to the amusement park together back in eighth grade. Then somebody told them the Wondercolts had limited spots for the Games. The girls went from having a conversation together to testing every conceivable way in which one of them might be better than the other. Arm wrestling was among the more recognizable events. There was pottery. By the time Lyra was doing a peacock impression and Sweetie Drops had committed herself to an owl, you could reasonably wonder which of these accomplishments Crystal Prep was best equipped to challenge. Vice Principal Luna put up the roster. Both girls had made the team. They fell into a hug.

Luna herself needed pictures for the school yearbook. Photo Finish took the assignment and her two helpers, Pixel Pizzaz and Violet Blurr, and set to work on the students at lunch, in the gym, and in the library. Complaints from the subjects began reaching Luna soon afterward. Then she saw the photographs. They were so good they quite interrupted the reprimand she’d prepared. Photo Finish, sensing that the occasion called for a portrait of the vice principal, turned her camera on Luna. It was one way to make sure everybody got something like equal treatment.

There was still a welcome banner to make. Luna wanted Crystal Prep to know their hosts were glad to see them and quite capable of giving them a run for their money. By the time she came back, the design involved sheet music, science, and a plea for peace. You could tell from the finished article that people at Canterlot had strong individual ideas. Luna liked it well enough to ask for several more just like it. It was going to be a busy afternoon before the Games even began.

Over at Crystal Prep Academy, Twilight Sparkle had been gathering evidence of an unexplained energy source at Canterlot High. This Twilight wore glasses, lived with a dog named Spike who’d been a dog his entire life, and had a quite reasonable expectation that investigating an energy reading would lead to more data. It led to a school full of strangers greeting her by name.

She’d built a device to measure the energy and hung it around her neck. At Crystal Prep she was good enough at her work to hope for a place in Everton’s independent study program. Solitude suited her research. It had also become the easiest way to get through a school day. Principal Cinch understood exactly how much that application mattered and used it to get Twilight onto the Shadowbolts’ team for the Friendship Games. The Wondercolts had never beaten Crystal Prep. Cinch intended to have every possible advantage on hand.

Canterlot High presented Twilight with some bewildering results. Rarity made clothes for her friends and lit up with magic. Pinkie tried to improve a rather grim welcome party and lit up, too. Fluttershy took time for Twilight when she was feeling wretched. The device drew in their magic, opened rifts between worlds, and gave Spike a speaking voice. Meanwhile, Sunset was trying to work out why the girls could suddenly pony up without touching an instrument. She wrote to the princess. This time an answer didn’t come when she needed it.

The academic round ended with a problem on the board and the two schools’ best hopes standing side by side. It was Sunset against Twilight. Twilight got the answer and won the round for Crystal Prep. The people who gathered around her afterward were girls in Wondercolt colors, congratulating her on the work. Across the room her own classmates had expected exactly this of her. She’d fulfilled the expectation. As a way of making a person happy, it had its limitations.

Over at the archery range, Twilight couldn’t hit her target. Her own teammate Sour Sweet had plenty to say about this, none of it much help to a girl with a bow in her hand. Applejack stepped over and coached her. She had perfectly good reasons to keep quiet. The teams were in the middle of a relay, and every extra second Twilight took was a second in Canterlot’s favor. But here was somebody struggling with a thing Applejack knew how to do. Once Twilight landed her shot, she hugged the girl she was supposed to beat.

Consider Twilight at the archery range, friend. The rules made Applejack and Twilight opponents, but the rules had not made them incapable of helping one another. There is a lovely distinction between winning a contest and becoming the sort of competitor who is worth playing with. Later, Sunset's offered hand makes that distinction much larger than the Games.

Sunset had a harder time being generous. During the motocross leg, vines reached through a rift and nearly got her. Rainbow put herself in harm’s way to help. When Twilight’s device drained Rainbow, Sunset rounded on its owner in front of everybody. Twilight tried to explain what she’d wanted to understand and ran off in tears. Sunset had good reason to be frightened. She also knew, almost as soon as she’d done it, how she’d sounded.

Cinch and the Shadowbolts urged Twilight to open the device and use what she’d collected. Under that much pressure, with the future she wanted on the line, she did. As Midnight Sparkle she could see into Equestria and pull the opening wider, even as the ground broke apart under the students’ feet. Down below, girls in Crystal Prep uniforms reached for girls in Canterlot colors. The score had ceased to interest anybody.

Sunset gathered her friends’ magic and rose to meet Twilight, bright against Midnight’s dark wings. She understood the terrible exhilaration of finally having all the power you’d wanted. When she got close enough, she offered Twilight her hand. That was something she’d learned at the bottom of a crater. Twilight took it.

Afterward, when she got a say in where she wanted to study, Twilight chose Canterlot High. She still had her glasses and her dog and an appetite for finding out how things worked. She wanted the chance to eat lunch with people who were glad she’d come. When Princess Twilight finally stepped through the portal and met her, there they were, two girls with the same face and quite a lot to catch up on. From here on, the Twilight carrying a schoolbag alongside the other six was the girl who’d chosen to transfer.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 06 · the friendship games

tracks.announcement_text:
There is more to discover about the girl from Crystal Prep, and the journey the seven friends will take to Camp Everfree.

Having the same face as a princess complicated the simple business of being the new girl. What if somebody expected this Twilight Sparkle to know all about friendship, too? Rarity, Pinkie, and the others had been having sleepovers for years. Twilight had to learn the rules of Sardines along with the much less explicit rules about what it meant if your friends kept talking when you left the room. A message from one of her old Crystal Prep classmates got her wondering what the girls might be saying. It took a little nerve, in a roomful of people having a perfectly easy time, to tell them she’d never been to anything like it before.

Twilight did what came naturally and took the question of friendship to the library. A quiz in a teen magazine attached quite a bit of importance to doing things such as swapping clothes and baking cookies. Twilight invited Sunset over to bake. They had some remarkable common ground for two girls measuring ingredients in a kitchen. Each had once gathered up more magic than she could bear. Each remembered what happened next. When Twilight offered to lend her boots as well, Sunset quite reasonably declined. They’d already had the part of the afternoon that mattered.

A quiz can only ask the questions its author thought of. It cannot account for two girls who know what it is like to have been frightened by their own magic, or the ease of sharing a kitchen without having to explain every part of yourself. My lilac tail curls quite contentedly at that thought.

Eventually Twilight invited the two sets of girls to get to know each other on easier terms. Applejack and Sunny Flare could put on country music and bake. Pinkie and Sour Sweet could discover just how thoroughly they agreed on the decorating possibilities of glitter. Twilight could host a sleepover of her own, with people who had once made it rather hard for her to get through a school day. There was no box on the magazine quiz for pulling that off.

The trouble with taking a bus to Camp Everfree was that Twilight could fall asleep on it. In her dreams Midnight still knew her name. Awake, with her friends around her and a whole week outdoors ahead, Twilight had enough to think about. Then things started moving without her touching them. Of all the people at camp who might have been delighted to discover telekinesis, it had to be the girl who could remember tearing holes in the world.

The others found out about their abilities under circumstances that allowed considerably more room for comedy. Applejack was spotting Rarity on the climbing wall. The line caught, Applejack gave it a pull, and Rarity shot up with a speed that suggested some urgent revisions to their understanding of Applejack’s upper-body strength. Applejack caught her coming down. Rarity, quite ready to handle her own harness after that, threw out a hand and sent Applejack into the water with a glittering diamond-shaped shield. Both girls owed each other an apology, although it was difficult to say what either ought to do differently next time.

Pinkie was decorating cookies when her sprinkles started exploding. Fluttershy wanted paper towels for the cleanup. A bird obliged, and Fluttershy realized she could understand it. Rainbow went for a climbing harness and made it almost all the way back to town. Then her speed gave out. There was a stretch during which she had to get back to camp the slow way. If you wanted to measure the range of the new powers, Rainbow had volunteered an impressive amount of data.

Sunset learned about hers at night. Twilight had packed her things and slipped out with Spike. The sensible thing, as Twilight saw it, was to take whatever was wrong with her as far away from her friends as she could. Sunset followed. When she touched Twilight, she could feel the fear and see what Twilight had been remembering. It was an intimate power to acquire by surprise. Even with that glimpse, the rest of the conversation still required two people. Twilight had to say how afraid she was of Midnight. Sunset had to ask her to stay.

I find Sunset's decision to ask Twilight to stay especially moving. Her magic lets her perceive something private, yet it does not make the conversation unnecessary. Knowledge and companionship are not interchangeable. Even with a glimpse of another's pain, one can still ask, and listen, and leave room for an answer.

Somebody else at camp was scared. Gloriosa Daisy knew how much this place meant to the families who came back to it. She also knew what she owed on it, and how close she was to losing it. She’d been using enchanted geodes she found in a cave to keep everything going. A problem with the camp would come up, somebody would call for her, and she’d promise she could handle it. Her promises were getting larger. So were the accidents. By the time she took the last of the geodes and became Gaea Everfree, she was trying to keep the camp safe by sealing the people she loved inside a wall of thorns.

To get them out, Twilight had to reach for the power she’d spent the week trying to shut away. Her friends called to her. She could hear them and the memory of Midnight at the same time, and she chose what to do with her hands. She pulled the geodes free. Each of the seven girls came away with a pendant and a power she could carry home.

A magical rescue left one thoroughly ordinary problem. Gloriosa still needed money. So they put on the Crystal Ball in the cave. Former campers turned up for a place they remembered loving, Rarity got a splendid occasion to dress people for, and the Rainbooms played. For once Gloriosa got to see what happened when people found out she needed help and had enough notice to show up.

Back at school there was a crack in the pedestal of the Wondercolt statue. A little Equestrian magic was still slipping through. In the days ahead it could turn up in the least imposing objects. Canterlot already had a pretty good understanding of magical crowns. A watering can was going to take everybody by surprise.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 07 · the other side of fear

tracks.announcement_text:
A dance competition, a film studio, and a small enchanted mirror await us, friend.

Rarity once put money her friends had already raised into materials for a music video they had yet to shoot, for a competition they had yet to win. She had everyone’s agreement. Twilight made sure everybody understood the arithmetic of losing. Still, when you picture Rarity bent over a torn jacket afterward, consider how much of her friends’ trust she had sitting in her sewing basket.

They were trying to pay for repairs at Camp Everfree. Rarity had come across the Chance to Prance competition and told some Crystal Prep girls what she had in mind. Then she saw Sour Sweet, Sugarcoat, Sunny Flare, and Lemon Zest practicing her idea. They were good dancers. Back at Canterlot High, Sunset had put her heel through Rainbow’s jacket during rehearsal. Even before the question of credit came up, there was the uncomfortable possibility that the other girls could do a better job with Rarity’s idea.

Rarity tried confrontation. She tried asking the band for other concepts. Applejack proposed apple fritters, Rainbow had a Daring Do chase in mind, and Pinkie’s idea involved outer space. Anyone who’s ever asked friends for help with a project will recognize the experience of receiving three enthusiastic answers to an entirely different question. It was a dance competition. Rarity eventually went out for ice cream.

Rarity could have kept her idea to herself and considered the other girls' failure a victory. Instead, she discovers a collaboration that neither group could have made alone. It is a rather satisfying instance of harmony, friend: each party remains itself, and both acquire a possibility that was absent before.

That was where she heard the Crystal Prep girls talking. They had the steps. They needed an original song. Their classmates were expecting a spring dance on a yacht, and they had rather given the impression they could pay for it. Rarity could have had a fine few minutes listening to their predicament. Instead she went over to their table. The Rainbooms could write and play. The Shadowbolts could teach them the routine. If they won together, there would be enough prize money for both schools’ plans. They did win. And somewhere in the work, Sunny Flare and Fluttershy had got down to the much more interesting business of improving a lyric together.

Rainbow once got so far into a Daring Do book in her bedroom that Applejack honking outside became a sound in the jungle, and Twilight’s ringtone came out of a parrot. When Twilight and Rarity went upstairs to find out what had become of her, Rainbow was on top of her wardrobe. She was supposed to be going to the movies. Now Canter Zoom, who was directing a Daring Do picture, had invited the girls onto his set in thanks for the camp fundraiser. Rainbow could walk into a room and recognize the things a prop maker had built from the descriptions in her books. Juniper Montage knew the studio just as well from a different direction. The director was her uncle. When she pictured the girl playing Daring Do, she could see herself in the costume.

Chestnut Magnifico, the actress who did have the part, had other work coming up. A little delay on set could mean a big change in casting. Things started breaking, and props approved by the author began disappearing. A studio was a tricky place to chase somebody in a disguise. It was an excellent place to have Rainbow on hand to notice which details belonged in a Daring Do adventure. The girls worked out who had the access and the motive. Juniper lost her place at the studio. The girls earned small parts in the picture, which only made Juniper’s view of the situation worse.

At the mall cinema, where she had a new job, Juniper acquired a hand mirror touched by Equestrian magic. In its glass she could see herself as the star she wanted to be. A wish that some spilled popcorn would clean itself up made the popcorn disappear into the glass. Then a wish about some people worked the same way. Soon all seven friends were trapped inside, and the person left to help was a visitor still getting used to having fingers. Starlight Glimmer had come through the school portal with Sunset, who’d gone home to replace her filled-up journal. Starlight knew a thing or two about making a grievance so large that other people got hurt living inside it. She offered Juniper friendship. She also asked her to make good on the offer by letting the girls out. Juniper had to want to undo what she’d done. With her own hands back, Sunset had one more person she could introduce to the others.

A mirror is a curious object to recur in these stories. It may show what one wants to become without showing what becoming it will cost. Juniper has much in common with Sunset, though they are not the same person. I am glad Starlight asks her to act on the friendship she is being offered.

Once Daring Do’s picture was playing at the mall, Apple Bloom, Sweetie Belle, and Scootaloo went back for another look. They called themselves the Canterlot Movie Club. Before they’d even made it into the theater, Pinkie turned up in considerable distress. Somewhere in the course of buying candy she’d lost Gummy, the little stuffed alligator she took around with her. A girl carrying a plush animal is generally the best judge of how irreplaceable it is. The three took the case. Their search carried them from the lobby clear out to the trash cans, an unpromising place to look for anything you hoped to give back to somebody. They spotted him behind glass, sitting among the prizes in the claw machine. Scootaloo took the controls. It took her a few tries, but Pinkie got her particular alligator back. Then the club went in to see what sort of adventure Daring Do was having.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 08 · a dance and a mirror

tracks.announcement_text:
Let us wander around Canterlot High for a while. Not every memorable day there begins with a magical emergency.

One Monday morning, Twilight and Sunset both had to get to school in a downpour. Twilight got herself ready in good time. Sunset overslept. Getting out the door on schedule conferred surprisingly few benefits once the weather got into the act. At school the other girls looked as though they’d had much the same trip. Pinkie took a picture of everybody. There had been a time when both Twilight and Sunset would have dreaded somebody taking a picture of them looking like that at school. This one they could laugh over together.

Pinkie once tried coaching Fluttershy as a cheerleader. They began on the sidelines of a soccer game, where a certain amount of volume was undeniably useful. Things went better when they worked their way around to cheering for a chess match. Here, finally, was an event at which everybody could appreciate the considerable skill with which Fluttershy could cheer under her breath.

Twilight once had the rare pleasure of hearing that the principal herself would be teaching geology. Celestia missed teaching. Here was a classroom, here was a student who would have been delighted to answer a question about rocks, and for a few seconds they had each other’s undivided attention. Then Miss Cheerilee needed Celestia in the library. Then Granny Smith needed her in the cafeteria. Then there was the repeated sound of Rainbow’s soccer ball hitting the outside wall, which was difficult to pass off as a geological disturbance. The telephone rang. Every time Celestia came back she tried to pick up the lesson. About the only bell in the building that could still have interrupted her was the one that ended class. Right on time, it did.

Twilight had a project of her own going at home. There was a stormy night of diagrams, computer code, and machinery in her home lab. At the end of all that labor Twilight unveiled a robotic puppy for Spike to play with.

Twilight making a robotic puppy for Spike is a delightful little image. I find myself smiling at the care concealed inside all those diagrams. The grand magic at Canterlot High has its place, but so does an evening spent making something that one particular friend will enjoy.

Rarity had a magazine at lunch with a picture of Countess Coloratura taking a tumble in yoga class. Imagine having a bad five seconds and then having people who’d never met you discussing it over lunch. Each girl could supply an incident she was happy to have kept out of print. Applejack and Pinkie had burnt pies so thoroughly that they’d set the sprinklers off. Rainbow had managed to take down an entire display of soccer balls at work with one well-aimed kick. Fluttershy had let birds do her hair. Twilight could remember a lab mishap that had left Spike as thoroughly covered in muck as she was. Over lunch they managed to give one another the impression that embarrassments like these scarcely ever happened to them. Then they all got up, encountered the same patch of wet floor, and went down in a heap. At least everybody with a firsthand account was in the pile.

Give Pinkie a surprise to plan for someone else and she could start immediately. Ask her to paint whatever she liked and she could spend half an art class deciding on a subject. In art class Sunset was happily painting sunflowers. Pinkie had a blank canvas. Sunset suggested getting her creative juices flowing, which sent Pinkie off in search of a drink. She tried looking for inspiration outdoors. She tried her drums. Eventually Sunset suggested painting something that made her happy. Out came the paint, in considerable quantities. When Pinkie was finished, there on the canvas was Sunset herself. Sunset got paint on Pinkie by giving her a hug.

Once, Sunset spent a miserable stretch of time at the mall waiting to buy a new video game. Rainbow spotted her alone in that endless line and put her speed to the modest, excellent use of rounding up their friends. They kept Sunset company until she finally reached the counter. The game had sold out. Pinkie, it turned out, had preordered a copy for her weeks ago. For a girl so often accused, with reason, of getting distracted, Pinkie could remember something you wanted long before you had occasion to ask.

She and her sister Maud made an interesting pair. Maud could hold forth on rocks in a voice so even you might miss the depth of feeling involved. When she gave a talk at the natural history museum, Pinkie, Rarity, and Twilight lent her some magical special effects. The audience perked up. A young admirer wanted Maud’s autograph. Growing up with Maud must have been quite an education in all the different ways a person can sound delighted.

Applejack and Rainbow could find competition anywhere, including the school yearbook. Applejack brought in a pig for the Young Farmers’ Club photo. Rainbow mentioned how many clubs she belonged to. Applejack belonged to one more. Soon they were joining clubs for the purpose of appearing in more pictures than the other girl. Rarity, who had sensibly pointed out that membership in school clubs was a peculiar thing to compete over, had an exclusive fashion club of her own. When the yearbook came out the two competitors were tied. The pig, meanwhile, had become vice president of Rarity’s club.

During her internship at Prim Hemline’s boutique, Rarity had to design a window for a visiting Fashion Week scout. Imagine putting your work behind glass on the street where you live. Anybody could stop there and make up their mind about it, including the person who’d given you the job. Rarity took a walk with Sunset. On the way she admired some work by the street artist Flanksy. She got back to her own work, finished the window, and still went home unhappy with how it had turned out.

In the morning there was a crowd at the glass. Somebody had worked on the display overnight, and Prim Hemline, for one, loved it. A little way off stood Sunset, with a dab of paint on her cheek. Rarity recognized the work and then, rather wonderfully, the artist. Think of Sunset on that walk the day before, getting to hear what her friend thought of her art while Rarity had no idea she was talking to the person who’d made it.

I rather like Sunset being quietly pleased that Rarity admired Flanksy's work before knowing who had made it. Recognition can be pleasant for reasons entirely apart from a name. And sometimes a friend sees a quality in us that we have not quite found a way to discuss with them.

There was a complication of making a start in fashion that you could predict by looking at the calendar. An invitation to a designers’ gala could arrive on a night Rarity had already promised to babysit. For that predicament she knew just whom to call.

Lily Pad wanted to read her book. Pinkie, who’d come over to babysit so Rarity could go to the gala, had quite a few activities in mind. Sitting quietly while somebody else read hadn’t made the list. Lily was perfectly content. It was Pinkie who needed entertaining.

Eventually Pinkie asked what she was reading. Pirates, as it happened. Lily started explaining what was going on, and Pinkie found herself acting it out. They could have the evening Lily wanted and there was a part in it for Pinkie after all. By the end, Lily was reading aloud and Pinkie was falling asleep. Pinkie thought Lily had done a lovely job looking after her.

Fluttershy helped get the girls’ pets ready for a charity calendar to raise money for the shelter. There was bathing to do before there were pictures to take. Pinkie’s stuffed alligator Gummy qualified for inclusion, which tells you something about the entry requirements. Sunset wanted to help and kept looking at her friends with their pets. Eventually she admitted that she’d like one of her own and had no idea how to choose. Fluttershy took her to the shelter. You could introduce Sunset to any number of appealing animals, but the one she lit up for was a little leopard gecko. She named him Ray. He made it into the photographs.

At the animal shelter, Fluttershy could put on a concert. Give her a song and a roomful of animals and you could hear what the Rainbooms had in their songwriter. Give her a roomful of students waiting for an audition, and standing up to sing could be a much bigger proposition. Those two things fit together quite comfortably if you knew Fluttershy. She loved to sing. She liked to know who was listening.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 09 · ordinary days at canterlot

tracks.announcement_text:
A little magic has been finding its way into some rather ordinary things. Our next adventure begins in a garden.

Twilight took her own watering can to Principal Celestia’s garden. Celestia was going on vacation. The job called for someone who would remember to water the plants, and she had got herself a volunteer who considered it an opportunity to study botany. Spike came along. Somewhere between the start of the job and the first watering, a little loose magic found its way into the can. Twilight sang while she worked. From down among the leaves came a perfectly audible answer.

It’s easy to see how she got herself into trouble. If you give a plant a drink and it grows before your eyes, of course you’re going to want to try that again. Soon Twilight had a whole garden singing back at her. The plants grew big enough to do their own reaching, and they had definite ideas about who ought to keep that water coming. Twilight sent an urgent message to Applejack. It was Applejack who saw what was going on with the can. With the garden sprinklers running instead, the plants settled down. Celestia got her warning about the dangers of overwatering in a little late.

At school, Sunset was having trouble with the part of her magic that let her feel what somebody else was feeling. Until then it had generally required touching the person. One day she could walk through the hall and pick up everything from Sweetie Belle’s anxiety about a science project to the little tune Trixie sang about herself inside her own head. Earmuffs were hopeless. Sunset tried to ask her friends whether anything odd was happening to them and heard their answers while they were still trying to work out how to tell her.

The sudden amplification of Sunset's gift raises an interesting question for a cosmic unicorn. More information is not always more understanding. The moment she has access to everybody's feelings, it becomes much harder to attend to any one of them. A conversation needs space, including the space in which a friend chooses what to share.

Then Rainbow arrived from the soccer field, remembered her backpack, and made the trip all over again. She was finding an extraordinary number of reasons to run somewhere these days. Twilight thought the girls’ geodes might be charging one another up every time any of them used hers. That possibility made the arithmetic of saving a few seconds on fetching a backpack look considerably different. They agreed to give the powers a rest. Rainbow even managed to leave an awkward conversation at walking speed. Sunset got to have a quiet head again.

There were things you could do with seven girls’ worth of magic that did absolutely nobody any harm. Sunset drew a comic about the lot of them going into the city. She gave Pinkie a brand-new pastry to look forward to, then had a thief run off with a jeweler’s stock before anybody could have dessert. She knew her friends well enough to draw Fluttershy politely asking for the jewels back in the middle of a chase. The band had let Sunset in on their rehearsals. Now they could see the adventures she got up to with them when she was alone with a pencil.

In Cranky Doodle’s math class, having a gift for talking to birds could be something of a liability. Fluttershy was trying to sit a quiz. A few birds had fallen out over the division of sticks for their nests, and one is perhaps unwise to settle an argument out loud using numbers when there’s a test paper on the desk. Trixie accused Fluttershy of getting answers. Fluttershy went up to the board and worked a problem for herself, with the whole class watching. Later, alone with the birds, Trixie put in a request for some tutoring.

Fluttershy had a different use for her friendships with small creatures when Twilight had a long-anticipated evening at the planetarium. She sent her off with a jar of bugs, a peculiar addition to an otherwise meticulously planned outing. By the time Twilight discovered that an exhibit was gone, the show was canceled, and clouds hid the actual stars, her careful preparations had run their course. Out came Fluttershy’s fireflies. They arranged themselves into constellations in the dark.

Suppose you were in Sunset’s position. You’d traveled between two worlds, performed in front of the whole school, and just failed your driving test. Mr. Cranky Doodle wanted her to practice with somebody experienced before her last chance on Monday. She had three offers. She really ought to have asked what everybody drove before she picked.

With Rarity she’d get a stretch limousine for the day. Rarity had given considerable thought to the ideal volume of the music and the preferences of a thirsty passenger. Sunset would have to explain that she rather hoped to sit up front and steer the thing. Fortunately the chauffeur, Randolph, could teach her. With Applejack she’d get Granny Smith’s pickup and a flat tire. That lesson would come in very handy when Mr. Doodle’s car suffered the same indignity during her retest. He’d see Sunset reach straight for the jack. Fluttershy could offer her own car and a rhyme for remembering all the things to do before setting off. Come Monday, Sunset could run through it for herself. Anyone who’d been on the road with Fluttershy would have understood why Sunset might choose her. Being meticulous about what happened before a car began to move was rather a reassuring quality in a passenger.

I confess, friend, that the image of Sunset having to explain to Rarity that driving practice involves sitting in the driver's seat makes my mane bounce with amusement. Fluttershy's attention to the small preparations seems rather wise. There is something reassuring about a person who has thought of the ordinary things.

Twilight could look at a perfectly legible message made up of pictures and feel an urgent need for a dictionary. Rarity could pick up the phone and carry on in fluent emoji. Fluttershy found she could express herself quite fully with a selection of animals. Sunset had a third suggestion, one that easily got overlooked in discussions of all the things a phone could do. You could use it to call somebody.

On the school news, Rarity’s problem was having to announce the next big trend with nothing especially promising in her purse. She could take inspiration from Twilight, whereupon glasses and books would sweep the school. By the time Twilight wanted something from the library, everybody else would have beaten her to it. Rarity could apologize and direct public enthusiasm toward capes. If she took inspiration from Rainbow, the halls would fill with rainbow wigs. Rainbow would be quite comfortable in a school full of her doubles. Rarity, repeatedly greeting the wrong person, would have a rather longer day. And if she put Pinkie in charge of deciding what everybody needed, the answer would be confetti. Principal Celestia would only have to open her office door to find out how thoroughly the trend had caught on.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 10 · magic in the garden

tracks.announcement_text:
There is a play to put on at Canterlot High, and Fluttershy has an audition to get through. I rather like this part of their story.

The girls all wanted to try out for the fall play, Dazzled. You could go to auditions with six friends. The catch, as Fluttershy discovered, was that when your name came up, you still had to walk out there on your own.

How she might manage it depended on whose hand she took first. Rainbow could put her behind the microphone at a soccer game. At first the crowd would be lucky to hear a word. Once the ball started moving, Fluttershy had something to tell them, and some of that feeling could go with her into the audition. Applejack’s suggestion was to picture the audience as chickens. Fluttershy could do even better with that advice than Applejack expected. After her successful audition, she’d admit that the faces she’d imagined all belonged to Applejack. With DJ Pon-3, she could make her entrance amid lights and music splendid enough to keep an audience happy however softly the girl in the middle spoke.

It was quite a play to have brought out such nerves. Rarity got to be Selfie, a coal-town girl who’d set her heart on becoming a disco dancer at Club Amethyst. Twilight put on an old lady’s voice. Rainbow was the Fairy Bootmother. Someone had to see that the bedazzled footwear turned up on cue and that the cast could arrive in Shiny City without anybody spotting two students struggling to move the city across the stage. That someone was Sunset.

At rehearsals Twilight had promised to run lines and help Applejack with the stage. The list went on. Sunset could see she needed a break, and what a break might look like depended on which friend took her away. With Fluttershy in a meadow, she could keep worrying for a while, but Fluttershy had animals to introduce, and eventually Twilight would fall asleep in the grass. With Rainbow she could try running and a succession of sports, to the considerable surprise of the athlete she’d go on to beat. Pinkie’s method would be to keep reappearing with ideas until Twilight devoted her entire attention to wondering where Pinkie would pop up next. By Pinkie’s reckoning that would be a successful afternoon. Twilight would indeed have spent it thinking about something else.

Then Sunset discovered a boot missing. Rarity took the case. If she questioned Pinkie, she could have a confession almost at once, hampered only by the fact that Pinkie had an alibi and quite a different offense on her conscience. A straightforward request to point out the boot would locate it under the bell-bottoms. If she questioned Trixie, both girls could conduct a tense interrogation without either saying a word. Rarity could hold out long enough to do her makeup. When Trixie finally made a move, a trail of loose studs would lead to Spike, who’d wanted to try dancing in the boot. If she asked Applejack, she’d be sent directly to the costume rack. There she’d find Maud contemplating the amethysts. The danger with leaving the case to a dressmaker and a rock enthusiast was that Sunset would have to come and fetch the evidence while both were still admiring it.

The Shiny City scenery posed a harder problem. If Sunset called Twilight over, she might expect the backdrop to float into position. Twilight would have a perfectly good robotics-club project to try out on the job. Pinkie could build a whole new city out of balloons and take a fair bit of weight off the stage crew that way. Micro Chips would have his own ingenious contribution. He could persuade Bulk Biceps that operating the ropes was good exercise.

There was quite enough actual carpentry left for Applejack, the only person who’d applied to be set designer. Then she brought a hammer down on her hand. The nurse expected her to recover nicely provided she stayed away from practically every task that had to be done by Friday. If she handed the work to Rainbow, she’d have a nerve-racking time watching someone build at tremendous speed with scarcely a glance at the blueprints. The result would turn out better than the plans. On a sheet of green paper at home, Applejack had drawn the set she’d really like to make if only she had the time. Rainbow had run over to get it.

Pinkie could take the same job and keep her promise to practice her drum solo. Applejack would just need to direct her to wherever the next nail had to go. Or Applejack could hire Photo Finish, in which case she’d find very little resemblance to her drawings even after the work was finished. Photo Finish, Violet Blurr, and Pixel Pizzaz had built their design around lasers. Applejack would have to wait for the lights to go out to see what she’d got.

On opening night, Fluttershy had one line. She had to ring a bell and announce that the mine was closed. Applejack encouraged her from backstage. Everything went beautifully until the bell came crashing down. Now there was Fluttershy in the very situation she’d dreaded at auditions, a whole room watching to see what she’d do.

My hoovsies would be very firmly planted backstage for that bell. What I love about these possible endings is that Fluttershy's friends do not all help in the same way. The important thing is that the help leaves a space in which Fluttershy can say the line herself. The applause belongs to the girl who has actually said it.

If Applejack stepped in, she could come on disguised as a tree and lift the bell. If Sunset signaled to Twilight, the bell could rise by itself, which would leave Fluttershy just enough to do with her hands to get her voice back. Or Sunset could walk straight out there and improvise an earnest account of what she thought the play meant. The longer Sunset had to keep talking, the better Fluttershy’s chances of being the second most embarrassed girl onstage. Whichever friend she took her cue from, Fluttershy got her line out.

Apple Bloom, Sweetie Belle, and Scootaloo had put together a slideshow about making the play. What they lacked for the afterparty was a projector. Mr. Doodle took excellent care of his and intended to keep on doing so. Applejack could meet him in a contest of endurance, leaving the younger girls to walk off with it while the two of them stood their ground. Rarity could conduct a courtroom cross-examination on the finer points of who actually owned school property. He’d come to the party with his projector under personal supervision. With Rainbow helping, the younger girls could report a mathematical emergency in the gym and send their teacher rushing off to help while Rainbow took care of the equipment. The trouble with inventing a mathematical emergency was being expected to stay and do the math problems. For three girls who’d already done quite a bit of work on an evening off, Rarity’s offer might have been worth a second look.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 11 · one line for fluttershy

tracks.announcement_text:
The Rainbooms have a performance to get to, and Applejack has found a vehicle. Come along, friend.

A band with an engagement to get to eventually had to answer the question of how all seven girls and their instruments were supposed to get there. Applejack found them a bus. It made it into the parking lot, which was an achievement the girls could appreciate more fully once they’d seen the state of it. Twilight started working out what it would take to make it roadworthy. Having somebody who could lift the bus was a tremendous convenience. So was having friends who could work at speed, decide what the finished thing ought to look like, and get paint where it was needed. They made a tour bus you could recognize as theirs from halfway across a parking lot. There’s something endearing about how completely their idea of having a band had changed since those first rehearsals. Somebody had to play bass. Somebody also had to find transportation.

The Rainbooms had promised to play at Cousin Goldie’s party. Before the bus moved an inch, Twilight had accounted for the instruments, the directions, and the precise number of seconds they could afford to remain parked. She trusted the GPS to allow for traffic. Applejack’s granny, who was driving, had her own views about which road to take.

A tour bus makes a surprisingly good picture of harmony. Twilight's careful planning, Applejack's practical skill, Rarity's eye and the others' particular talents have to fit into one physical object. It is more interesting than a bus made by seven identical people. And Granny Smith's route, well, that is an entirely separate matter.

The flat tire took Applejack and Twilight between them. Fluttershy got out to negotiate with the cattle that were standing in the road having lunch. A fallen tree was very much Pinkie’s department. That left the broken bridge. Up front Granny put her foot down. It would have been a remarkably bad time to discover that Granny had misjudged the distance. As it happened, the bridge belonged to a film crew and was going to need replacing by the props department. Pinkie managed an appreciative word for their work on the way through.

They made it. Goldie introduced the Rainbooms and got to ask Granny how the drive had been. It's a pity she couldn't also have asked the woman who'd been expecting to get a day's shooting out of that bridge.

With finals coming up, Twilight took the time to work out how each of the others studied best. She understood that being told to concentrate was of limited use to a girl who already wanted very badly to pass. Two weeks was enough time to try something that fit each person. At Crystal Prep, time to study had often meant time away from people. At Canterlot High it could mean sitting down with the whole group.

Fluttershy wanted to get some of the animals at the shelter adopted. She set up a camera, took a breath, and ran into a difficulty entirely new to the animals she’d gathered. The puppy could look like himself in front of a camera all afternoon. Fluttershy, who could talk to anyone about finding a pet, began an introduction addressed to animals who might be looking for a home. Trying again somehow got her onto the question of whether the viewer’s home was furry.

When Twilight begins thinking about how her friends learn, she is doing something that the solitary student at Crystal Prep seldom had occasion to do. She is adapting her knowledge to the person beside her. And Fluttershy's commercial works for a similar reason: her friends recognize something worth showing in the footage she considered a failure.

She moved behind the camera. This took care of one problem. The animals she was trying to film began playing up and wandering out of shot. By the time Twilight and Applejack arrived, Fluttershy thought the afternoon had been a wash. Her friends wanted her to have another look at the footage. What would you want to see if you were thinking of bringing a pet home? A dog being his affectionate, disreputable self could make an excellent case for being wanted just as he was. Fluttershy had a commercial. It needed a little editing.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 12 · the rainbooms on the road

tracks.announcement_text:
Let us spend some time with Sunset and a girl named Wallflower Blush. Their story concerns the curious nature of memory.

Sunset worked on the yearbook. It suited a girl who’d come to care about having a place at this school. She could put somebody’s picture on a page, get the names right, give people something to take home. She and her six closest friends had been voted best friends. Wallflower Blush worked on the yearbook, too.

Wallflower had been at Canterlot High for years. She tended the school garden. She was the entire gardening club. While everybody was remembering the extraordinary distance Sunset had come since the Fall Formal, Wallflower had ample opportunity to observe how rarely anybody remembered meeting her. Sunset didn’t think she’d ever really mistreated Wallflower. From her end of the yearbook office, that had seemed enough.

Then Sunset turned up to meet her friends at the beach and found herself facing the five girls she’d bullied. They knew her perfectly well. What had gone missing was everything good that came afterward. For Twilight, who’d come to school later, one of the memories left to go on was Sunset shouting at her during the Games. Try telling that girl that you were also the person who came after her in the woods at camp. Sunset could remember both of them. Twilight had every reason to back away.

The journal still worked. Princess Twilight remembered her. In Equestria, Sunset finally stood before Princess Celestia again and apologized to the teacher she’d walked away from. She’d had a long time to dread that meeting. Celestia welcomed her, and then the two of them could get on with helping Twilight and Princess Luna search the archives. They found an account of a Memory Stone. Someone on the other side of the mirror had been choosing which pieces of a life other people were allowed to keep. Sunset went back to investigate. The princess stayed with the books and uncovered a deadline. By the third sunset the losses would be permanent.

Back at school it was Trixie who stood by Sunset. This took some sorting out, since Sunset had suspected Trixie in the first place. Trixie had demanded a yearbook superlative commensurate with her greatness and power, got nowhere, and made a satisfyingly ominous exit. Now she was willing to help investigate. The yearbook was still open to negotiation. Trixie could genuinely care about somebody while keeping a firm eye on the publicity.

Wallflower had come upon the stone while gardening. Initially she’d used it to take back embarrassing moments. It must have seemed an enviable trick to a girl who went home remembering every awkward word she’d said. Except that if people kept losing the memory of your attempts to talk to them, what chance did they have of knowing you better the next day? She watched Sunset with her circle of friends and used the stone to erase the good they knew about her. In the yearbook office, Sunset and Trixie went so far as to look for suspects without thinking to question the other person sitting in the room.

When Sunset learned the truth, she got angry enough for Wallflower to have reason to fear her. Wallflower took away the last few hours from both investigators and left them locked in the yearbook room. Sunset had anticipated this possibility and left a camera running. On the recording she got to see her own face as Wallflower had seen it. Trixie, beside her, wondered how often anybody had gone out of their way to be kind to the girl. Sunset had counted on being able to prove she’d changed. Here, at last, was a chance to do something about the hurt she could see.

Of all the magic at Canterlot High, the Memory Stone gives me particular pause. My nature has a certain affinity for the idea of continuity, friend. Removing the uncomfortable part of a record also removes the chance for another person to understand what happened next. Sunset's friends recover the painful memories as well as the happy ones, and that is what allows them to know the person who stands before them.

Trixie also got a moment she’d been waiting for. She pulled off her escape trick and got Sunset out, only to find herself locked inside. She told Sunset to go on. By then Sunset had told Trixie how much it meant to know she would still have one friend tomorrow. Trixie could have gone home happy on the strength of that alone, once somebody let her out of the yearbook room.

When Sunset caught up to Wallflower, she tried to talk to her about what it had been like to be overlooked. When Wallflower turned the stone on the others to take away their memories of high school, Sunset stepped between them. For a few moments she couldn’t remember coming through the portal or meeting anybody on this side of it. The girls who’d been afraid of her moments before saw her do that for them. They reached for her, their geodes lit, and together they broke the stone.

Everybody got their memories back, including some that it hurt to have. Then the yearbooks came out. Trixie got her acknowledgment. Wallflower’s garden had visitors and her book had signatures. Imagine how it felt opening that book later at home. She could have read it again the next day, too. The names would still be there.

On the last day of school, Rainbow and Twilight were keeping time to the same bell with rather different hopes for what it might do. Twilight had thank-you notes to write to her teachers and extra-credit work to finish. Rainbow persuaded Miss Cheerilee to show a Daring Do movie. Twilight kept working through it. To her considerable dismay, the bell rang before she could finish.

Rainbow, whose feelings about being released for the summer were quite uncomplicated, found the thing to say. Twilight could read any book she liked now. The library would be open. Think what it meant that Rainbow had thought of that. Somebody else might have told Twilight to put her books away and enjoy the weather. Rainbow sent her into summer excited about her own idea of a good time.

Rainbow did not have to become a bookworm to offer Twilight a lovely summer. She only had to remember what would make Twilight happy. I find that a very affectionate use of friendship, precisely because the two girls need not enjoy their holidays in the same way.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 13 · the girl they kept forgetting

tracks.announcement_text:
School is out, and some of the girls have work to do. Let us see what becomes of their summer plans.

If you showed up at the Apples’ for a barn dance, you got the best part of Applejack’s day. You got the music and the company and the barn all ready to go. Come earlier and you’d get a better idea of what it had taken to have you over. There were animals to tend, work to finish, a barn to prepare, and somewhere in there Applejack had to get herself ready, too. Put Granny Smith, Big Mac, and Apple Bloom in the picture and you got a little closer to how she understood a good evening. She liked having people under the same roof. That meant getting up early even on a day that would end late.

Her hands went from farm work to the bass guitar to a shift at the mall juice bar. That last job could get dull. You could be sincerely fond of apples and still have had about enough of making the same drink by mid-shift. One day a beet turned up among her ingredients. Applejack started experimenting with combinations, made a little show of mixing them, and drew a crowd. Rarity usually got the credit for spotting possibilities in raw materials. It would have done anybody good to see Applejack with that beet.

If you only knew Pinkie from parties, you might have missed this about her. She was genuinely interested in what other people liked. At the Sweet Snacks Café, she could take one look at a customer’s order and start figuring out what kind of day they’d had. A girl with a stain on her dress could use Rarity. A swimming team sore about a loss could use some encouragement from Rainbow. Pinkie put people in touch with each other in the course of getting them something to eat. After taking care of everybody else, she was quite capable of needing someone to notice that she’d like a sundae herself.

If you took a book along to the Sweet Snacks Café and hoped to read it in peace, there was a chance Pinkie would let you. Your odds went down considerably if the person in the next booth was reading the same book. She spotted two customers who bumped into each other and then sat apart, each deeply occupied with a copy. You could have let those two discover their common interest for themselves. Pinkie had a diner at her disposal and an ice-cream sundae within reach. By the time both customers were wearing some of the ice cream, they’d had a proper look at each other’s reading material. They got up to dance. The book had provided a perfectly good introduction. It had taken Pinkie a surprising amount of ice cream to make it.

You could follow a favor quite a distance around the mall on a day when the girls were working. Trixie found a practical use for being able to pull a rabbit out of a hat. Fluttershy had been looking for that particular rabbit. Across the mall, Twilight fixed DJ Pon-3’s turntable. Soon there was music outside the clothing shop where Rarity had been having no luck whatever attracting customers. Rarity in turn spotted a pyramid of shoeboxes coming down on Rainbow at the sporting-goods store and put a diamond shield where it would do some good. When the strap on Sunset’s sandal broke outside the sushi place where she worked, Rainbow was exceedingly well placed to find her a pair of sneakers. By the fountain, Sunset found somebody who could use a little company and shared the sushi she was carrying. Quite a few people went home owing their improved afternoon to somebody they hadn’t even seen.

All these favors travel through the mall like small signals whose origins the recipients may never discover. No one needs to know the entire sequence for the goodness of a particular act to matter. My silver sigil glimmers at the thought of a day made slightly easier by so many ordinary choices.

Rarity and Applejack had applied for the same summer job at Equestria Land. They were going to stand together and sell caramel apples. Rarity freely conceded that Applejack had the more relevant résumé, a sensible judgment from anybody who’d ever met an Apple. While they were practicing how calmly they would answer the phone, the park emailed them both. Applejack had been turned down. They wanted Rarity to design the costumes for the light parade.

Rarity offered to decline. Applejack told her to take it. Both girls meant what they said. Applejack also wished she were going too, and Rarity was tremendously excited about having a real design job. Neither feeling did their friendship any discredit. Having to keep up the impression that there were only uncomplicated feelings involved was where it got exhausting.

Rarity's excitement and Applejack's disappointment can both be sincere. I appreciate that this story gives them room to feel both things. A friend need not extinguish her joy in order to acknowledge another's hurt, and a hurt friend need not pretend to feel nothing in order to wish her well.

Working in the costume room at Equestria Land, Rarity ran into a difficulty you could have missed if you only visited on parade day. Some days she could look straight at the same materials that had always suggested a dozen things to make and find herself without a single idea she wanted to use. This was still her job on those days. She stayed with it long enough to find a dress worth making. The people who eventually got to see it could have had very little idea how long she’d spent at the beginning with nothing to show.

Rarity’s new boss, Vignette Valencia, had an audience for everything, right down to her lunch. An encounter with stray Equestrian magic had given her phone the ability to make actual things disappear and to project improved versions. The first casualty was a salad. By opening night she’d taken an interest in the Rainbooms. She could put them in her parade. And if a girl had some objection to the image Vignette had picked for her, well, there was the phone.

Meanwhile, the girls had a whole amusement park to get around. Fluttershy was nervous about the big coaster. Rainbow went along while she worked up from a much smaller one. When they finally took the big ride, Rainbow got a good scare herself, and Fluttershy was the one in a position to appreciate how brave she’d been. Elsewhere, Twilight and Sunset encountered a ring-toss game. Sunset recognized a racket. Twilight understood the physics. Between them they had sufficient expertise to explain, in some detail, how they were losing all their tickets.

While Rarity had a crew to direct and a deadline to meet, friends began vanishing. Applejack took her suspicions about Vignette to Rarity and had the galling experience of telling the truth to a person who knew she was jealous. Rarity had heard some uncharitable things about a woman who’d handed her an extraordinary opportunity. Applejack had a missing friend to find and couldn’t get Rarity to take five minutes away from the parade to help. The conversation went as badly as you’d expect.

When Vignette proposed taking Applejack’s place on bass, Sunset refused to play without her. Pinkie had to remind Vignette that their friend’s name was Applejack, and Twilight was quite prepared to vouch for her honesty. All three wound up in the same blank white space as Fluttershy and Rainbow. When Vignette showed Rarity the replacements she planned to project in their place, Rarity went looking for Applejack. Together they called their missing friends. Applejack opened a door, and there they were. The mysterious white space was a room in the park. Entirely possible to spend ages fearing you’d been banished to a different dimension and then discover that your friend can let you out. The girls destroyed the phone, and the actual Rainbooms played the parade. Vignette, for all the people who followed her, could think of remarkably few people she could call friends. Rarity still had it in her to offer her a start.

They’d applied to Equestria Land hoping they might spend the summer side by side. When Rarity took the stage, she had Applejack there on bass.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 14 · a summer at the mall

tracks.announcement_text:
Our friends are at the beach now. Twilight and Pinkie are about to make a rather unexpected discovery about the measurement of friendship.

When Pinkie found a friendship quiz in a magazine Rarity had left on her beach chair, Twilight’s first concern was that she hadn’t studied. Still, she could surely answer a few questions about Pinkie. Favorite food? Cotton candy was a reasonable guess. Third place, as it turned out, behind cupcakes and cake. Pinkie’s idea of Twilight’s favorite food was books. Her own favorite part of school was helping the janitor refill the snack machines. There was some quite new information in this little exercise for both of them.

They scored a spectacular pair of zeroes. Pinkie was prepared to put the magazine down. Twilight had just been informed, in print, that she’d failed at being this girl’s friend. She went to work on the beach with enough equations to settle the question properly. When the tide rolled in and washed her work away, Pinkie was distressed on her behalf. She’d spent the afternoon quite happy to keep a friend company while she did the math. Twilight had all the answer she could use by then.

Oh, Twilight. My mane swishes with affection, friend. She is a girl who can turn a beach into a blackboard when she thinks she has failed a friendship test. Pinkie already knew she was having a fine afternoon beside her. There is no need to make an equation out of every good thing, even if the equation would be beautiful.

There was plenty to do at that beach, including getting a considerable distance from your towel without ever going near the water. Sunset came upon a bottle containing a treasure map. She and Pinkie and Twilight followed it to a chest, which held a further clue and a decoder ring. Somebody had even laid out a trail of seashells. They tracked down the rainbow on an ice-cream truck and the treasure at the sushi truck beyond it. For all that ingenuity, they had earned twenty percent off a hand roll and as much wasabi as they cared to eat. Pinkie was delighted. A little less wasabi would have suited her fine.

A mark in the background of a group selfie required another outing. Sunset and Pinkie saw the possibility of a sea monster. Twilight wanted a better look. Fluttershy went into the water and came out with the stranger that had appeared in their photograph. It was Pinkie’s inflatable flamingo. The real animals at the beach required enough attention as it was. One day Fluttershy heard hatchling sea turtles calling. She explained that it mattered for them to make their own journey to the water. Rainbow, Applejack, Rarity, and Fluttershy set to work clearing a path. While the girls were busy making sure the little ones could manage the trip, Rainbow’s tortoise Tank went on ahead with them in tow. As far as his young charges were concerned, Tank was their mother. It was a pretty emotional farewell for a fellow who’d gone to the beach with Rainbow Dash that day.

Pinkie once set off for shaved ice while her friends were trying to find homes for some crabs. A little boy dropped his treat. A gull helped itself to another. Hot sand complicated the return journey so considerably that it involved a beach ball, umbrellas, and a kite. The crabs ended up with the last of the ice, which was as well because the heat was making them decidedly cross. Rainbow took one look at the state of refreshments for the humans and made a second run.

You could also find Applejack working a shift as a substitute lifeguard or heading out on a surfboard with Rainbow. Fluttershy was quite candid about letting the more experienced girls take the waves. Her brother Zephyr had more difficulty admitting he’d never done this before. It took one outing alongside Applejack and Rainbow before he was ready to ask Rainbow for a lesson. She agreed to give him a few pointers. Having your bluff called by your sister’s friends could have ended considerably less well.

The day Twilight took Rarity and Pinkie sailing, she’d memorized a nautical dictionary. Rarity had packed a change of clothes, some tools, gems, and a fashion reference library. The luggage stayed ashore. Out on the water the wind surprised them and Twilight lost her map. Pinkie raised a wave with her magic and got the boat back to the pier, where all three could stand dripping and appreciate Rarity’s foresight on one point. She’d brought towels.

Rarity once lost one of the earrings she’d made. She was at the beach with Applejack and Rainbow, putting on sunscreen, when she discovered a bare ear. It took some distress on Rarity’s part and a gentle invitation from Applejack before she could actually ask her friends to look for it. She had already got them metal detectors. By sundown they had a heap of curiosities and Rarity felt terrible about wasting everybody’s afternoon. Applejack was interested in what might be buried in the half of the beach they hadn’t searched yet. Rainbow had another go. In the end it was Rarity who found the earring, tangled in her own hair. The three of them had spent the day to within inches of it.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 15 · friendship math

tracks.announcement_text:
A new school year brings a new timetable. Even seven girls with magical powers can have trouble finding a lunch period together.

On the first day of a new school year, the girls compared timetables and discovered how efficiently a person could be separated from her friends without leaving the building. Applejack had art. Fluttershy had drama. Twilight had physics. Nobody seemed to have anybody. Principal Celestia had given the students until the end of the day to request changes, and six of the girls took her up on it.

The first rearrangement landed Rarity in wood shop, Rainbow in home economics, and Pinkie in advanced physics. They went back. This time they asked for just one period together. Celestia managed lunch. They were sitting there enjoying the one class at which everyone could reasonably expect to excel when somebody noticed the empty place. Sunset had gone to the principal’s office about her schedule. Celestia had the expression of a woman who had devoted quite a considerable portion of her day to the eating arrangements of seven teenagers.

There were days when sharing lunch scarcely seemed enough. Rarity once asked Rainbow to come over after school. Rainbow said she had plans, then took off on her motorbike with Twilight. Rarity hailed a taxi. Having always wanted the opportunity to tell a driver to follow somebody, she now had the miserable experience of arriving at the shops and finding more of her friends together without her. She asked him to take her home. He had to point out that she still needed to tell him where she lived.

It took a little time for Rarity to learn what that closed bedroom door was hiding. I am fond of the difference between a secret intended to exclude someone and a secret intended to welcome her. The same fragment of evidence can look quite different when the missing part of the afternoon finally arrives.

When Rarity opened her bedroom door, there they all were. They had been putting together her surprise birthday party. Rainbow had gone to some trouble to make sure that Rarity had people to come home to that afternoon. Rarity recovered sufficiently to insist she’d known all along, and her friends were kind enough to let that go with a laugh and a hug.

Pinkie, who could so often read a face across a crowded café, had her own spectacular failure of interpretation. Sweet Snacks had a run of five-star reviews on an app called Screech. A woman came in, ordered coffee, settled down with her newspaper, and gave the place four. You could practically feel Pinkie lay the loss of that last star at her own feet. She went on offering the woman food and attention. She could have saved herself a great deal of running around if she’d considered how many times her customer had tried to get back to the paper. Eventually Pinkie let her read. Up went the fifth star. This must have been one of the harder services for Pinkie to master. It required remaining on the other side of the room.

Homecoming preparations once landed the whole group in detention. Pinkie had decorations, Twilight had a pie-making robot, Fluttershy had gerbils, and Rarity was recording her outfit of the day. You’d have had a hard time working out from those facts alone how Mrs. Harshwhinny ended up wearing an apple pie, which was rather the problem facing the girls in detention. Each remembered the person responsible for the calamity immediately in front of her. Rarity’s recording included the people on either side. By the time they’d put the whole chain of accidents back together and convinced their teacher that nobody had set out to prank her, detention was over. Rarity’s outfit, at least, had received a most exhaustive viewing.

With Rarity, Applejack’s affection tended to take the form of something you could use. She set out to build her a dressing room and record the process as a do-it-yourself tutorial. A building job with Rarity contributing suggestions as it went along was hardly the easiest choice for a first-time viewer to follow. But you could see why these two kept undertaking things together. Rarity could imagine having a place of her own to get ready. Applejack knew how to build it. They were going to have opinions about every inch.

Spend enough time being the person people come to for help with animals and they can get the idea they know everything you’re good at. Sunset invited Fluttershy onto her gaming channel to introduce her to video games. Fluttershy picked one with squirrels. The idea was to collect nuts in a basket, and in short order Fluttershy was doing exceptionally well at it. Sunset, who had expected to spend the session explaining things, grew visibly frustrated. Eventually she settled in to watch Fluttershy play. By then the people tuning in to Sunset’s channel were getting to know both girls rather well.

Fluttershy choosing the squirrel game makes me smile. A friend may have an ability that our familiar picture of her has left out. It is a small delight to discover a new part of someone we thought we already knew rather well.

At one of Trixie’s street performances, Twilight saw a use for telekinesis that would have bewildered the examiners at Crystal Prep. A little real magic went into the act. She let Trixie keep the applause.

Expertise didn’t help much at the planetarium when Twilight found herself in the same room as Rosette Nebula, an astrophysicist she admired. She knew the science perfectly well. It was walking up and introducing herself that got her. Pinkie tried to help and managed to make being inconspicuous practically impossible. Later there was chocolate cake, and eventually Twilight did get to talk to Rosette. Pinkie naturally drew her own conclusions about the cake.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 16 · another year at canterlot

tracks.announcement_text:
The girls have been finding new ways to share their interests. Come with me, friend, to the Canterlot Pet Show.

Fluttershy sounded as if she were reading someone else’s handwriting when Applejack introduced her as cohost of the first annual Canterlot Pet Show. Then a Boston terrier barked. Fluttershy brightened. His name was Banana, he liked bananas, and he had a toy banana he was particularly fond of. Another dog confided a weakness for daytime television. The camera was still on, the audience still there, but Fluttershy had stopped thinking about what to say on camera. She wanted to know what the next dog had to say.

By the time Applejack needed to wind things up, Fluttershy was asking for one more interview. It was Winona. Apple Bloom had brought the family dog along to compete, a secret Winona herself had wanted to keep from Applejack. Fluttershy got to deliver the surprise and send them off together. She closed the broadcast herself.

The microphone had not grown less intimidating in the instant that the Boston terrier barked. Fluttershy had simply found someone she was interested in hearing. Her attention moved toward the little creature instead of toward the audience's judgment. I can appreciate that as a radio host, friend. There is a wonderful difference between wanting to be heard and having something one wants to share.

During the victory lap she had the inside word on Tank, who had helped Rainbow win second place despite being in love. Applejack looked impressed by the reporting. Apparently Tank was a chatty fellow if you happened to speak tortoise. Micro Chips and his robot took third. Cranky Doodle and his dog Fluffersnuff won, a fine comeback by a dog whose mood during the personality round had left something to be desired. Gummy, Pinkie’s stuffed alligator, remained one competitor whose private thoughts Fluttershy could never quite get at.

Gummy had rather more to say when Pinkie supplied the voice herself. She recorded a cookie lesson in which Gummy praised her and helpfully reminded her to leave some chocolate chips for the dough.
