Tank attended as well. It was quite a feat for a tortoise to get near an ingredient before a girl who moved at Pinkie’s speed had whisked it away. She worked two kisses from him into the recipe and made sure he got a finished cookie.

Back at Twilight’s house, Spike had ordered a deluxe package of dog supplies for his own viewers. It included a flying disc much too delicate to throw and a used sock that Spike considered the highlight. Twilight had found the receipt. Two hundred dollars was a lot to spend on the pleasure of smelling someone’s foot. The items went back into the box, in front of the same audience that had just seen them come out.

There was room on the girls’ feeds for things that went wrong, too. Rainbow tried hiding in Pinkie’s locker to give her a scare and wound up as the frightened party. An attempt at a bottle flip could end with Principal Celestia showing the students how it was done. Rarity let people see the outtakes from her own song, and Applejack let them see hers. It gave you a rather different impression of somebody’s poise when you’d seen what happened before the take she kept.

Rarity even tried filming summer street fashion on an autumn day. Applejack, Fluttershy, and Rainbow all agreed to model. The clothes looked lovely. Their legs were cold. The arrival of snow settled a production decision for Rarity. She could make the next one indoors.

A dog chased a cat, Pinkie lost her balance with a tray of cupcakes, and Twilight’s coffee went flying. For most people on the sidewalk, those events belonged to the same untidy second. For Rainbow it was quite enough time to find the dog’s owner, put the cat in Fluttershy’s arms, steady Pinkie, arrange the cupcakes back on the tray, and send the coffee back into the cup.

You could understand why she sometimes got impatient. When Rainbow sang “Run to Break Free,” she described what it felt like to walk through school at everybody else’s pace. Even a perfectly agreeable afternoon stretched an awfully long way for a girl who could clear a truck in a single leap. Yet here she was using all that time to save someone a clean shirt. You could blink and come away with the impression that your coffee had behaved itself.

Rainbow's speed gives her time to do things that nobody else will even notice. I find that a much lovelier use of her extraordinary gift than winning another contest. Somewhere there is a girl going about her morning with absolutely no idea how close her coffee came to a very different destiny.

When Applejack asked Rainbow to help out on the farm, Rainbow took the assignment seriously. Unfortunately it was also the day A. K. Yearling was signing books. Rainbow could see her way clear to keeping both commitments if she allowed hardly any time for doing the chores. She ate up the work with her super speed. She hadn’t allowed for the Apples wanting to sit down over cider, and she couldn’t understand why Applejack seemed hurt when all the work was getting done.

Applejack and Big Mac could manage the farm. What they scarcely got to do anymore, given homework and the occasional emergency downtown, was spend an afternoon with Rainbow. The invitation had seemed quite clear from their end. Once Applejack found out about the signing, she went along to the bookstore. They were late for the event, but she caught Yearling on the way out. Rainbow got her book signed and the two girls still had the evening together. Next time she heard that a friend had some leaves that needed raking, she might want to leave the whole afternoon free.

What Applejack wanted was not a farm that had finished its work earlier than usual. She wanted the afternoon with Rainbow. The distinction is easily missed when one is trying very hard to be useful. A shared hour sometimes matters more than all the tasks that could have fitted into it.

The school later offered prizes for individual sports and one for the best athlete overall. Rainbow’s friends trained for different events. Fluttershy beat her at discus. Twilight beat her at ping-pong. Rarity had her in ballet. And so it went until Rainbow had a pile of second-place medals and a perfectly genuine claim on the overall title, which brought her surprisingly little comfort. It took an exhibition soccer match to draw her back out. She had advice about who to put where. Her friends could do some fairly spectacular things, especially once their captain started taking pleasure in how good they’d become.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 17 · the microphone and the afternoon

tracks.announcement_text:
There is a great deal of energy in Rainbow Dash. Let us follow her through a few of the adventures that put it to good use.

The invitation to play Blitzball at school came with one condition that stopped Rainbow cold. Coach Comet Chaser wanted boys only on his team. Rainbow challenged the league to play against the girls. She wanted any girl who could play to get an honest tryout. Once the match was under way, she noticed something odd about the opposition. They could barely keep going. Double practices for two weeks had done a remarkably good job of draining the pleasure out of their sport. Rainbow, ahead on points and in reach of what she’d come for, proposed that both sides call a tie. The coach walked out when his own players stood up to him. With help from a teacher, they could put together a school league where they had a say in how they played. As a route to getting on a team it was fairly involved. As an afternoon spent figuring out what a captain owed the other people on the field, Rainbow could hardly have done better.

Think back to another occasion after the Friendship Games. Canterlot High and Crystal Prep put on a joint science fair, and Twilight had the opportunity to work with students who remembered her as the girl with the private research project. This time she and her partner built a device to get people dancing. They tested it with Rarity and Pinkie, and the Rainbooms supplied an original song, “Get Up and Dance.” Fluttershy wanted the other students on backup vocals. At the demonstration even the principals got moving, a sight worth turning up for whatever you thought of the science. The project placed second. Plenty of people could say they’d had a hand in it, including the girl who wanted everybody else on the recording.

I like that Rainbow eventually sees the tired boys as people rather than as obstacles between her and the victory. Winning the right to participate is important. Making a game that everyone can enjoy is another accomplishment entirely. Her friends' science fair shows a similarly pleasant change in the meaning of a successful result.

Working together was a little harder on a shift at Sugarcube Corner. Pinkie liked the chance to tinker with a cupcake recipe and to know the person across the counter. When Rarity joined as cashier, the two friends discovered they had quite different ideas of good service. Then a chain bakery opened across the street. There was now a very practical reason to figure out what they could give a customer at their little shop that she couldn’t get by crossing the road. Friendship got them both behind the counter. The actual work of getting along had to happen there, one customer at a time.

At school, Rainbow had ten minutes before a championship soccer game against Crystal Prep and no idea where she’d put her lucky sock. Sunset tried to give the credit for Rainbow’s accomplishments to the person standing in front of her. Pinkie thought playing sockless sounded fine. Rainbow, who had to go out there with the team counting on her, would still quite like a sock.

My ears twitch with amusement. I do understand the comfort of a familiar little object before an important undertaking. But Rainbow has been carrying the skill she needs with her all along. I would not, however, recommend borrowing Bulk's sock.

Rarity could sew her a new one and set it with enough gems to briefly dazzle the opposing players when the sunlight hit them. Trixie had the advantage of a magician’s hat full of surprises. Give Rainbow Trixie’s lucky sock and the thing could take an active interest in directing her foot toward the winning shot. She could also borrow Bulk’s. He’d been preserving its luck by leaving it unwashed, which would do remarkable things for the amount of space everybody gave Rainbow on the pitch. Whichever sock she put on, it was Rainbow who had to keep her nerve long enough to score.

Rainbow Dash kept a tortoise named Tank. They went to the skate park together and recorded tricks. Set that beside the guitar solos, the soccer games, her delight in Daring Do, and the look she could get when somebody said an activity was too difficult, and it becomes possible to predict how she’d spend a spring-break cruise. She had six friends with extraordinary powers, an ocean of possibilities, and very little interest in the concept of time off.

Her friends had distinctly more interest. Applejack would have been happy just to get her stomach to agree with the motion of the ship. Twilight thought there ought to be some stretch of water where a perfectly sound scientific explanation for an odd light could get a fair hearing. Rarity had even set a location alert on her phone for duty-free shopping. Rainbow heard it go off and thought they were under attack. It was going to be a long cruise.

On the Luxe Deluxe the girls filmed themselves singing “I’m on a Yacht.” Pinkie got a rap break, dolphins leaped, and there was plenty of room for a girl with a new outfit to let the wind catch it. They looked utterly pleased with themselves. It’s worth keeping that picture of the trip alongside the memory of the lifeboats. They had come on board with music and a plan to enjoy the sea.

Rainbow really did see something shining out at sea. Unfortunately she’d spent enough time looking for a menace that her honest account sounded much like her wishful thinking. By morning she’d taken a lifeboat and gone after it. Sunset and Twilight followed her to an island. They found her sinking into what looked like quicksand. Sunset discovered that the sand concealed a portal to Equestria.

There were now two girls experiencing pony legs for the first time in company with Sunset, the original pony who had long since got used to sneakers. Rainbow had wings to consider. Twilight had a horn. In Ponyville, Princess Twilight helped identify what Rainbow had seen. It was a trace of the Storm King’s magic, enough to put a ship in real danger.

Rainbow had to hear that it was tiring to be recruited into one of her adventures. Twilight had to live with the fact that a friend whose conclusion sounded ridiculous had made an accurate observation. With the ship in trouble, neither girl had much to gain from a long discussion of who’d been right first. They took the Storm King’s staff back through the portal and quelled the storm. The ship was still sinking. Applejack freed passengers trapped in their rooms. Fluttershy turned up with life jackets for the petting-zoo animals. Pinkie went after the chef who’d banned her from the buffet. Rarity and Twilight got the passengers onto a lifeboat of their own making, and Rainbow put her speed to work getting them to shore. In the midst of it all, Sunset helped a frightened little girl find her mother.

The journey through the island is a particularly curious meeting of the two worlds. Sunset knows something about both forms of life, yet she still has friends experiencing the crossing for the first time. Rainbow's observation matters; so does Twilight's caution. When the ship needs them, both contributions can find their place without either girl having to win the argument.

The passengers still needed a way home. Taking them through Equestria meant Princess Twilight wound up with a castle full of unexpected ponies. It was an ambitious solution even by the standards of Canterlot High school trips.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 18 · a game and a voyage

tracks.announcement_text:
The Starswirled Music Festival is coming up. The girls have a great many things to pack, and Sunset has one particular performance in mind.

Applejack and Rarity put together some advice about what to bring to the festival. Applejack had sunscreen, hand sanitizer, toilet paper, and a sleeping bag in mind. Rarity favored a parasol, a privacy screen, and pillows in quantities that raised a practical question about how she expected anybody to carry them. Then she showed Applejack the RV. Both sets of recommendations suddenly made perfect sense. They were going to the same place and sleeping in entirely different sorts of luxury, at least in their heads.

Their friends had a say about what to wear. Rainbow wanted enough room to dance. Applejack stood by boots that had seen some use. Nature supplied Fluttershy with some charming little birds. Rarity rather fancied they had gathered out of an appreciation of fashion. Fluttershy could translate what they wanted, which was a meal of worms brought up specially for them. Twilight recommended ear protection and enough equipment to find your way back. She had even thought about both kinds of compass. There wasn’t the slightest danger of mistaking one girl for another once they had all dressed themselves.

It warms me that Sunset is as pleased to meet a lighting technician as a performer. A concert has many kinds of magic in it, and some of its most essential work is done where the audience never thinks to look. As a radio host, I have a particular appreciation for such invisible labor.

Twilight’s little camera drone went to Starswirled with them. Sunset got a backstage pass and took it along. Given access to the people behind PostCrush, she got tremendously excited about meeting the woman who ran the lights and the man whose work on reverb she recognized. Spending time in a band had given Sunset a whole additional set of people to be starstruck by. It’s lovely to think of what it meant to the crew to have somebody ask for their picture in a room full of performers.

Pinkie borrowed the drone to show people her favorite queues. The wait for nachos gave her ample opportunity to weigh the toppings before choosing all of them. The photo-booth line gave everybody time to practice a pose. She recommended one line without the slightest idea where it led. The bathroom queue, she felt, had all the people it needed to become a conga line. You began to understand why it could take the better part of a morning to get across the festival grounds with her.

Everyone wanted a say about filters when Sunset took a picture of them together. The girls experimented until Pinkie came up with a party picture complete with cake. Sunset liked it. Fluttershy liked the look of the cake. Applejack wanted the name of the filter so she could use it herself. Pinkie had gone ahead and decorated the actual space. The cake looked good for the soundest possible reason.

The act Sunset most wanted to see at the Starswirled Music Festival was PostCrush. Pinkie loved them, too. K-Lo on vocals and guitar, Su-Z on drums, the two of them back together onstage. Sunset had the occasion all laid out in her head. Pinkie could see quite a few things worth stopping for between breakfast and the stage. Where Sunset saw the risk of losing their spot, Pinkie saw a day out with her best friend who, as a bonus, loved the very same band.

Things got sticky around a churro cart. They got thrown out and missed the show. Pinkie tried to apologize. Sunset, bitterly disappointed, made sure Pinkie knew whose fault she thought it was. She went to sleep after missing the evening she’d wanted and woke up with the whole first day of the festival ahead of her again.

To begin with, that was a marvelous piece of luck. Sunset could allow for every delay. When that failed she could simply go without Pinkie. She got a spot right up front. PostCrush came on. The thing she had wanted so badly really happened, and Pinkie had to spend the day knowing that her best friend would happily have it without her. In the morning the day started over. The only person in the group who could remember what Sunset had done with all those chances was Sunset.

She even tried taking Rarity’s RV away from the festival. It broke down. Eventually she wrote to Princess Twilight, who identified the likely cause as an Equestrian artifact called the Time Twirler. Adagio, Aria, and Sonata were at Starswirled, singing a song called “Find the Magic” about one day running into the next. It was an unfortunate choice of title for anybody trying to convince Sunset of their innocence just then. Sunset had reason to ask what they knew. The Dazzlings had lost their magic at Canterlot High and were getting by without it. Adagio could be thoroughly unpleasant and still be telling the truth. Of all people, Sunset might have appreciated how it felt to be the first suspect on the strength of something you’d done a long time ago.

When Sunset put some effort into enjoying the things Pinkie wanted to do, she found she could have a pretty good day along the route she’d been trying to hurry them past. Eventually the two got backstage and met their idols. K-Lo and Su-Z had found the Time Twirler. If anything went wrong during their set, they could take the day over and play it better. Su-Z was tired. K-Lo could still think of things that might go wrong. From out in the crowd Sunset had been envying two musicians who had got themselves into an exaggerated version of her own trouble.

The Time Twirler gives the idea of a perfect day an unusually literal form. Suppose one could change the order of every event until the outcome looked precisely as intended. What might disappear in the process? Sunset eventually makes room for something that none of her earlier plans could have predicted. My lilac mane swishes with quiet delight at the thought that the imperfect day was the one worth keeping.

Getting that day back for everybody involved some difficulty with festival security, a remarkably hard churro, and one guard who remembered that Sunset had treated him decently. Pinkie knocked the Time Twirler free. Sunset smashed it. K-Lo and Su-Z now had to play a show straight through, with whatever mistakes happened along the way. Sunset and Pinkie got to play with them. There was no way either of them could have put that on the itinerary.

In the morning Sunset woke up to the second day. After about three weeks of yesterday, she wanted to spend it with Pinkie. For once they were in the happy position of having no idea exactly how it would go.

And Sunset got to sing at Starswirled herself. Rain came down on the stage and the crowd during “Let It Rain.” A wet audience can be a formidable sight from behind a microphone. Sunset stayed up there singing about weathering a bad stretch while the water fell on her too. By the end the storm was lifting. At the Battle of the Bands, she’d stood at the edge of the Rainbooms’ stage waiting for a sign that she belonged at a microphone. Here were people prepared to stand out in the rain to hear her.
tracks.title: through the mirror · 19 · a day at starswirled

tracks.announcement_text:
Let us linger at Starswirled a little longer. Each of the girls has her own favorite way to spend a festival day.

At Starswirled, the day you had depended a great deal on which girl you followed out of the tent. Take Sunset, still asleep after the all-night drum circle. In her sleep she was asking Princess Celestia for five more minutes before magic school. There were at least three good friends within earshot, each with a different idea of a good morning.

Go with Applejack and you could get to know the girl who set the campsite up every morning while everybody else slept. She’d even been rolling the sushi in the mini fridge. There were pancakes in Sunset’s immediate future, once she helped build the fire pit. Rainbow, meanwhile, had a series of yoga poses that got increasingly difficult to sustain on very little sleep. You had to stick with her long enough to see where she’d put you when the sun came up. That view was why she’d woken Sunset. As for Pinkie, she knew a breakfast involving waffles, cupcakes, sprinkles, and jelly beans. Sunset could have five gloriously energetic minutes with her and then a stomachache. When the sugar wore off, the drummer who’d helped keep the campsite awake all night was asleep herself.

Over at DJ Pon-3’s stage, the last drop of the beat was up for grabs. Take Sunset up with the DJ and the controls became an eight-bit game she could play, the little electronic sounds coming out over the crowd. Give Fluttershy the spot and she needed a minute. A festival stage is a long way from singing to the animals at the shelter. A few animals in attendance helped her find the beat, though, and by the time she let out a wolf howl there was very little doubt who’d made that sound. Or the DJ could hand a banjo to Applejack’s brother Big Mac. He had a way of making himself understood in very few words, and here he could dispense with the words altogether. It turns out a banjo will go quite nicely with a dance beat if the people in charge of both are willing to try.

Rarity had chosen suede and fringe for the festival. The rain took an interest almost as soon as she’d set foot outside. Applejack could find something good about a patch of fresh mud. She was thinking of fishing bait. Rarity, following the same sound principle, could see the makings of a mud mask. Twilight had thought up all kinds of protection against bad weather, although the materials immediately available to her were garbage bags. Rarity could make those into rain ponchos. Or she could call Vignette Valencia, of all people. Vignette took one look at Rarity’s wet hair and liked what the rain had done to it. With her encouragement, having your hair drenched at Starswirled could become the look everyone else was trying to get. It’s rather nice to think that, after all that trouble at Equestria Land, Rarity could still call Vignette with an extremely urgent question about her hair.

The mud also produced a small, bedraggled dog near the food trucks. Who got her back to her person depended largely on whom the dog took a fancy to. She could follow Rarity, who was perfectly willing to be friendly at a little distance and had considerable difficulty communicating the part about the distance. Retreating from a muddy puppy took Rarity all the way into the lounge where Su-Z of PostCrush recognized her dog. The puppy’s name was Princess Thunder Guts. Rarity’s reward for delivering her was a feather boa. If the princess picked Spike, the two dogs could fit a fair amount of eating and playing into the afternoon before their goodbye. Spike took it hard until she gave him a lick on the cheek. Fluttershy could shorten the entire operation considerably by asking the puppy who she belonged to. Su-Z got her dog back promptly that way, although Spike might reasonably have preferred the longer route.

All these festival afternoons remind me that a place has as many possible experiences as it has companions. One friend knows where to find the sunrise; another knows how to make a muddy morning into an occasion. Twilight's itinerary could be excellent on its own terms and still leave out a death metal show with Fluttershy. I am quite charmed by that particular discovery.

Applejack, who had been up early enough to make everybody else’s morning possible, wanted a good place at Dirk Thistleweed’s concert. She got right down in front, where somebody stomped on her foot. Rainbow and Pinkie helped her out of the crush. Applejack urged them to get back to the stage. She knew what they would be missing. They knew what she would be missing, too.

With Rainbow for company, Applejack could try a preparation Rainbow knew from her coach. The smell of it drew Dirk himself, seeking relief for a hoarse throat. Suddenly the girl who’d given up her spot in front had her favorite performer singing within arm’s reach. If Pinkie took charge, there was a wheelbarrow, a hill with a view, and finally Pinkie onstage personally nudging Dirk into Applejack’s line of sight. Or Applejack could notice Snips off by himself. He thought Snails had left him. She offered to keep him company. When Snails turned up with Dirk and an invitation to watch from the side of the stage, Applejack was there to share it. Sitting out a favorite song is considerably easier when you get some say in whom you sit beside.

Twilight had written an algorithm to fit the best possible route between bands into the available time. Her electronic planner couldn’t survive the quantity of sweat Bulk Biceps introduced into the equation. Spike and Twilight were obliged to see what somebody else thought worth hearing. There was Principal Celestia, spending the day with her sister Luna and Cranky Doodle. The three of them had been coming since the festival started. Twilight was so surprised to learn that her principal did things outside school that she practically said it to her face. Celestia could show her around, and by evening she was teasing Twilight about sending her a letter after every festival to tell her what she’d learned.

Following Micro Chips would turn up an equally good surprise. He had a second life onstage as MC Dex Effex. And following Fluttershy would mean going to hear Skull Cruncher, a death metal band. Fluttershy was a little nervous about what her friend would think of the music she loved. Twilight was willing to give it a go with her. Of all the musical discoveries that might have made it onto a meticulously planned agenda, how high do you suppose Twilight had ranked seeing a death metal show with Fluttershy?
tracks.title: through the mirror · 20 · the festival from many sides

tracks.announcement_text:
The girls have come home from the festival. Winter is approaching, and there are a few more memories I would like to share with you, friend.

The robot from the pet show gave everybody ample opportunity to notice the girls at work. Competing for a ribbon, JVJ-24601 had been manageable. When a much bigger, out-of-control JVJ came crashing into a concert at school, even its builder’s remote could do nothing with it. The girls got him out of harm’s way. The machine blasted them clear through the wall and onto the playing field, where Sunset discovered that her geode had fallen off. Once it was back in her hands the seven could bring the machine down together. There had been some doubt at the pet show over whether a robot qualified as a pet. From a school maintenance point of view, there was now a very good argument for entering a dog.

Pinkie Pie was a frozen yogurt shop’s thousandth customer. Her prize was one free topping. They might as well have asked her to pick a favorite sprinkle. Applejack liked fruit. Pinkie liked candy. Hand the decision to those two and Pinkie could choose candied cherries in the cheerful belief that she’d found a loophole, while Applejack quietly swapped them for fresh ones. Both girls would go home pleased with their cleverness. Ask Twilight and she could work out that chocolate-covered walnuts went beautifully with the flavors Pinkie had chosen. Unfortunately frozen yogurt keeps its own time while you’re doing the sums. Pinkie was perfectly happy to drink it melted. Fluttershy had explicitly asked to sit this decision out. She was animal-sitting, and the shop had rules. Open the door to consult her anyway and all the animals could come streaming in, the shop could get shut down, and a squirrel could supply the final sprinkle of acorn. That's quite a lot of excitement to get for free.

The frozen yogurt shop presents a surprisingly extravagant set of possible universes for one free topping. Some decisions really can be left to the pony or girl eating the dessert, friend. And perhaps Fluttershy's request to stay with the animals was already all the guidance her friends needed.

Another afternoon found Fluttershy, Applejack, and Rarity at Sunset’s place when they all got invited to Bulk’s costume party. Fluttershy knew she wanted to go. What she couldn’t picture was what she’d wear. Sunset had some truly alarming things in her closet and could turn a soft-spoken friend into a tentacled creature convincing enough to terrify their host. Rarity could spend ages putting together an exquisite princess dress, reveal at the last moment that she meant to wear it herself, then offer Fluttershy her pick of the dresses she already owned. Or Applejack could dig out a two-person pony costume. With Fluttershy at the front and Applejack bringing up the rear, neither would have to make the entrance alone. Of all the ways those girls had ever come into a room as a pony, this one definitely took the most coordination.

Winter at Canterlot High brought the usual collection of urgent seasonal business. Pinkie had seven minutes to deliver a soufflé to Rarity. Applejack’s family anticipated an attempt on their cider. Somebody had left the key to the toy donations at school. Any one of these could keep the seven girls quite as busy as a magical emergency.

There was also the morning they tried to manufacture a snow day after an unsuccessful night of studying. Pinkie built a snowman out of potatoes. Rarity knitted it a scarf. Sunset contributed a painted winter view, which was a considerable application of her artistic talents to the problem of an upcoming test. They got caught. By then they’d done an impressive amount of practical study on the subject of water vapor, which Rainbow had known they might need.

Take the soufflé. Pinkie baked one for Rarity every year, and every year it sank before she could get it to her. If you’ve ever watched somebody eat a thing you made especially for them, you know the little moment she kept missing. This year she’d worked out the timing. The obstacle she hadn’t factored in was a snowball fight in the front yard of such dimensions that getting a dessert across it required help from Sunset. With the minutes running down, Rarity came to Pinkie. She got to taste it in time. Pinkie finally got to see her do it.

At the Apples’, Twilight entered into the spirit of the cider-making party with a game-theory matrix. Flim and Flam had made something of a tradition of swindling the family, and this year she and the Apples were ready for them. A jug of salt-and-pepper water, an elaborate set of predictions about who would outsmart whom, and Granny Smith’s considerable enthusiasm for getting one over on the pair all came into play. It’s hard to imagine a nicer development for the girl from Crystal Prep than being asked to a family party where bringing a game-theory matrix made her an especially welcome guest.

For the toy drive the girls had a wagon and donations, and the donations were safely locked away. Sunset’s key was in her locker at school. The school was closed. Soon the proposals for getting in involved air vents, a cupcake diversion, and Applejack lifting the building. Twilight phoned Principal Celestia and asked if she’d open the door. The children got their toys. Later Twilight realized she’d left something else back at school, at which point the attractions of a well-planned heist appeared to be growing on her.

At the mall, Rainbow realized she’d forgotten to get Fluttershy a present for their exchange. She scrambled to find something that would suit her and came up with an instant camera. Fluttershy’s old camera had broken. It turned out she already had a replacement. Fluttershy already knew what she would do with two. She’d be able to take candid pictures of bear cubs from different angles. Of all the elaborate saves Rainbow had pulled off that year, this one came down to having a friend with unusually specific plans for photographing bears.

The photograph Applejack wanted was a little more formal. Her family had a tradition of taking a themed picture for the holidays, and she wanted one with these girls. She explained the cornucopia she had in mind. Rarity offered to see to the wardrobe. This was the moment somebody might have asked Applejack exactly what she meant by a cornucopia. Instead Rarity got to work.

Six girls dressed as produce had exactly until the bell to reach the auditorium unseen. They were still in the hall when it rang. There are things you do for a friend which you might prefer the rest of the student body never found out about.

My silver sigil glimmers with quiet affection. That holiday photograph is not the one Applejack initially imagined, yet it contains something the original plan could never have anticipated: a story all seven girls can tell. Perhaps the nicest thing about a shared memory is that it can have more than one voice and still belong to everyone.

Applejack was waiting in her regular clothes. She’d meant the cornucopia as a backdrop. By the time she’d finished laughing, her friends had a fairly clear idea of what she ought to wear, too.

Photo Finish took the picture. Applejack got her holiday card for the whole school, with all seven of them in it. If you wanted to know how they’d ended up dressed that way, you’d have to ask Rarity what she’d understood, Applejack what she’d actually said, and the other five about the walk down the hall. Pull up a chair for that part. Everybody remembers it a little differently.

And here we shall leave the girls for a little while, with the picture taken and the stories still theirs to share. Thank you for keeping me company, friend.
